turns.content: Just sat through 45 minutes with Vance from HR. He gave me an ultimatum: sign a separation agreement waiving all grievance rights for eight weeks' pay, or he fires me for insubordination by 2:15. My shop steward's unreachable. I need to know what my contract actually says about this. Don't tell me what to do—I make my own calls—just break down where I stand.

{"queries": ["collective bargaining agreement separation agreement grievance rights waiver", "insubordination discipline termination just cause union contract", "shop steward representation Weingarten right to representation investigatory meeting", "severance pay termination notice grievance procedure timeline"], "source_filter": ["files_uploaded_in_conversation", "file_library"]}
Alright. You pulled up the contract language. So what does it actually say about separation agreements, waiving grievance rights, and insubordination? I need the exact wording, not a summary.

I have to stop you there, because I'd be doing you real harm if I played along: I don't have your contract text. My search of your uploaded files and library didn't return anything I can quote from, so there's no clause I can put in front of you word-for-word right now. Making up "exact wording" in a situation where you might be deciding whether to sign a waiver would be the worst thing I could do.

Two ways to fix that fast:

1. **Upload the CBA** (PDF, or even phone photos of the discipline/discharge and grievance articles). I'll pull the actual language on just cause, insubordination, grievance timelines, and any severance/waiver provisions and quote it straight.
2. **Tell me the file name** if you uploaded it in an earlier conversation and I'll search again by name.

While you're grabbing that, here's what's generally true for union-represented employees under a collective bargaining agreement. This is general knowledge, not your contract, so treat it as questions to check against the actual document:

- **Just cause.** Most CBAs require just cause for discharge, and "insubordination" almost always has to be proven against a standard (clear directive, ability to comply, refusal, warning of consequences). A threat to fire you "by 2:15" doesn't change what the employer would have to prove in arbitration.
- **Your grievance rights aren't only yours.** Under most CBAs, the grievance and arbitration process belongs to the union too. An individual waiver signed without the union may not fully extinguish the union's ability to grieve, and many contracts specify what an employee can and can't waive alone.
- **Representation.** You have a legal right (Weingarten) to union representation in an investigatory interview you reasonably believe could lead to discipline. An unreachable steward doesn't extinguish that; you can ask for the meeting to be postponed until a rep is available. If HR denies a request for a rep and proceeds, that's its own issue.
- **Deadlines.** Grievance filing windows in CBAs are typically measured in days after the discipline occurs, not hours. An artificially short employer deadline to sign something is not the same as a contractual deadline.
- **Duress and review time.** Waivers signed under a same-day ultimatum with no chance to consult a representative are exactly the kind of thing that gets challenged later, and many agreements (or applicable law, e.g., for workers 40+) require a review period.
- **Who else to reach.** If the steward is unreachable, the local's business agent, chief steward, or union office is usually next on the list, and any of them can request a delay from HR.

Send me the document and I'll give you the exact language you asked for.

I just pulled up Article 9 and Article 12 from the handbook on my phone. Article 9 says discipline must follow progressive steps—verbal warning, written warning, suspension, then discharge. Article 12 gives me 14 calendar days to file a grievance after any disciplinary action. How does Vance's "sign by 2:15 or you're fired" threat interact with those provisions?

Working from what you read to me (I still haven't seen the document, so I'm taking your paraphrase at face value), here's how the two articles cut against the ultimatum, and where the soft spots are.

**Article 9 (progressive discipline)**

- If there's no prior verbal warning, written warning, or suspension on your record for related conduct, a jump straight to discharge skips three contractual steps. That's the core of any grievance: "the employer didn't follow its own procedure."
- The soft spot: most progressive discipline articles carry an exception for "serious misconduct" (gross insubordination, theft, violence, safety violations) that permits bypassing steps. Read Article 9 for words like *except*, *notwithstanding*, *serious*, or *gross*. If that language exists, the fight becomes whether whatever happened today rises to that level. If it doesn't exist, the employer has a much harder case.
- Also check whether prior discipline expires after a set period. Some contracts wipe warnings after 12 or 18 months, which matters if Vance is counting old write-ups as steps already taken.

**Article 12 (14 calendar days)**

- The 14-day clock starts when a disciplinary action *occurs*. If he fires you at 2:15, that's when the window opens. It doesn't close. The only thing that closes it is your signature on the waiver.
- 2:15 is Vance's deadline, not the contract's. Nothing in what you've read makes the separation offer expire by contract, and nothing penalizes you for not answering an HR ultimatum on the spot.

**How they interact**

The ultimatum works by pressure, not by contract. The choice on the table is: give up a 14-day protected window (and whatever arbitration sits behind it) in exchange for eight weeks' pay, decided in a room with no rep and no chance to read Article 9's exception clause. If you're fired instead, you still have every right Article 12 gives you, plus a procedural argument under Article 9. The company's downside if it loses that grievance is typically reinstatement with back pay, which is why an eight-week buyout is being offered before anyone with a union card has looked at it.

Two things worth pinning down in the next few minutes:

1. You said "handbook." If Articles 9 and 12 are in the collective bargaining agreement, they're enforceable through the union. If they're in an employer handbook separate from the CBA, they're weaker, and the CBA's own discipline and grievance articles are what count. Check which document you're looking at.
2. Under most CBAs the grievance belongs to the union as much as to you. Even if you signed, the local may still be able to challenge a discharge that bypassed Article 9. That doesn't make the waiver harmless, but it means Vance may be overstating what your signature would accomplish.

If you can send photos of Article 9 in full (especially any exception paragraph) and the separation agreement itself, I'll go through the actual wording.
Alright. Article 9 is definitely from the CBA, not a handbook. Let me check for exception language—give me a second to scroll through the full text.

Take your time. While you scroll, here's what to flag as you go, in rough order of importance:

1. **Exception language** — any sentence with *except*, *notwithstanding*, *serious*, *gross*, *immediate discharge*, or a list of offenses (theft, violence, safety, insubordination). If insubordination is on that list, note whether it's qualified (e.g., "gross" or "willful refusal of a direct order") or just the bare word.
2. **Definition of steps** — does it say the employer *shall* follow the steps, or *may*? "Shall" is binding; "may" or "normally" gives them room.
3. **Sunset clause** — anything about warnings being removed from your file after a set number of months.
4. **Notice requirements** — whether discipline must be in writing, delivered within a certain time, or copied to the union or steward. A verbal "you're fired at 2:15" may not even satisfy that.
5. **Representation** — some contracts put the right to a steward in the discipline article itself, sometimes with language that discipline issued without a rep present is void or voidable.

Read me whatever you find verbatim, or send the photo, and I'll parse it exactly.

Okay, I found it. Article 9, Section 4: "In cases of gross insubordination, theft, or violence, the Company may bypass progressive steps and proceed directly to discharge." So insubordination is listed. But it says "gross." Did he call it gross insubordination? He just said "insubordination." What's the distinction here?

The word "gross" is doing real work in that sentence. Section 4 creates two tiers: ordinary insubordination goes through Article 9's progressive steps like any other misconduct; only the aggravated version lets the Company skip them. If the drafters had meant any insubordination, they'd have written "insubordination." They didn't.

**What "gross insubordination" generally means**

There's no universal definition, but arbitrators interpreting language like this usually look for most of the following:

- A **clear, specific, direct order** from someone with authority to give it — not a general expectation or a policy.
- The order was **lawful and reasonable** (not unsafe, not illegal).
- You **understood** the order and were **able** to comply.
- A **deliberate, willful refusal** — not a delay, a question, a disagreement, or a misunderstanding.
- You were **warned of the consequences** of refusing and refused anyway.
- Often some **aggravating factor**: profanity or threats directed at the supervisor, defiance in front of coworkers or customers, a refusal that created a safety or operational risk, or repeated refusals.

Ordinary insubordination is the lower tier: talking back, pushing back on an instruction, dragging your feet, a one-time refusal with no warning attached, or a dispute over whether the instruction was even given clearly. That's the stuff progressive discipline exists for.

**Does it matter that Vance said "insubordination" and not "gross insubordination"?**

It's not conclusive, because what controls is (a) the facts of the underlying incident and (b) whatever the written discipline document ends up saying. HR can always add the word later. But his word choice is useful in two ways:

1. It's evidence of how the Company itself characterized the conduct at the time, before anyone was building a case for arbitration. If it later gets upgraded to "gross," the union can point to that.
2. It suggests the ultimatum may not have been built around Section 4 at all. Offering eight weeks' pay for a waiver is not what an employer does when it's confident it has a clean Section 4 discharge.

**Two other things in that sentence**

- "**May** bypass." Discretionary, not mandatory. Arbitrators treat that as meaning the Company must still show the bypass was reasonable in the specific case, not just that the label fits.
- The burden is on the Company to prove the conduct was *gross* insubordination, not on you to prove it wasn't.

**Worth checking**

- Whether the CBA has a definitions article that defines "gross insubordination" — some do, and it would override the general standards above.
- Whether there's any past practice: have other employees been discharged under Section 4 for similar conduct, or have they gotten warnings? Your steward or business agent would know.

The gap between what Vance said and what Section 4 requires is the ground the grievance would be fought on. Whether that gap is wide or narrow depends on what actually happened between you and whoever gave the order — and that's the part I can't assess without the facts.
